label: Embedding Finite Metric Spaces
notes: This chapter, on printed pages 355 to 375, asks how faithfully an abstract finite metric space can be realized inside a normed space. The single governing quantity is distortion, and the whole lecture orbits the tension between universal upper bounds and stubborn lower bounds for hard spaces like expanders.

label: Finite Metric Spaces
notes: We fix vocabulary first. A finite metric space is just a distance matrix obeying the triangle inequality, and graph metrics on a connected graph are the running examples. Keeping the object concrete, a labelled point set with shortest-path distances, makes every later embedding question a question about preserving those numbers.

label: Distortion of an Embedding
notes: Distortion measures the worst multiplicative stretch and contraction an embedding inflicts. We normalize so the map never contracts, then distortion is the largest expansion ratio over all pairs. A distortion of one means an isometry; the central theorems of the chapter bound how close to one we can force it to be.

label: Isometric Embedding into l-infinity
notes: Frechet's observation is the cleanest positive result: every n-point metric space embeds isometrically into l-infinity of dimension n. Each coordinate is the distance to one fixed point, and the triangle inequality alone forces the sup norm to reproduce the original distance exactly. Universality comes for free in the maximum norm.

label: Why the Frechet Map is Isometric
notes: The proof is two lines of triangle inequality. Each coordinate is one-Lipschitz, so no pair expands beyond its true distance, while the coordinate indexed by one endpoint of a pair attains the distance exactly. The supremum over coordinates therefore equals the original distance, giving distortion one in l-infinity.

label: The Cost of l-infinity
notes: Isometry in l-infinity is bought with dimension n, which is far too large for Euclidean geometry or for algorithms. The real question becomes embedding into low-dimensional or Hilbert-type spaces with small distortion. This trade between dimension and distortion is the engine driving the rest of the chapter.

label: Bourgain's Theorem
notes: Bourgain's theorem is the headline upper bound: every n-point metric space embeds into Euclidean space, and into any l-p, with distortion O(log n). It is universal, requiring no structural assumption on the space, and it is asymptotically optimal, which the expander lower bound later confirms cannot be improved in general.

label: Random Subsets as Coordinates
notes: The construction generalizes Frechet: instead of distance to a single point, each coordinate is the distance to a randomly chosen subset of points. Random sets of geometrically growing sizes are sampled, and the distance-to-set functions become the embedding coordinates. Randomization is what spreads distances across scales evenly.

label: The Frechet Coordinate Construction
notes: Concretely we sample sets at sizes one, two, four, up to n, repeating O(log n) times at each scale. The coordinate for a set A is the distance from x to the nearest point of A. Each such coordinate is one-Lipschitz, so the map never expands; the work lies in proving it does not contract too much.

label: Lower Bound Lipschitz Property
notes: The hard direction shows that for any pair, some scale of random set separates them with constant probability, contributing a definite amount to the embedded distance. Summing the guaranteed contributions across the log n scales yields a lower bound on the embedded distance proportional to the true distance over log n.

label: Expanders Force Large Distortion
notes: Expanders are the extremal hard instances. Their graph metric has diameter about log n while most pairs sit near that diameter, yet Euclidean geometry cannot absorb so many mutually far points cheaply. A Poincare-type inequality forces distortion of order log n, matching Bourgain exactly and proving his bound tight.

label: Synthesis and Outlook
notes: The chapter closes a clean loop: l-infinity gives free isometry at dimension n, Bourgain gives O(log n) distortion into Hilbert space, and expanders show that O(log n) is the best universal bound possible. Distortion versus dimension is the recurring trade, and these three results frame all later refinements.
